slides.title: The mixture question everyone ==sets up wrong==

slides.stem: A chemist mixes a $40\%$ acid solution with a $70\%$ acid solution to produce $60$ liters of a $52\%$ acid solution. If $x$ is the number of liters of the $40\%$ solution and $y$ is the number of liters of the $70\%$ solution, which system of equations represents this situation?
slides.hand: set it up, don't solve it

slides.body: One equation counts liters: $x + y = 60$. The other counts acid: $0.40x + 0.70y$ on the left, and on the right $52\%$ of the $60$ liters, which is $31.2$. Keeping raw percents like $40x + 70y = 52$ mixes units — percent of nothing equals a bare number.

slides.title: Amount = decimal percent × volume
slides.body:
In any mixture, the substance amount is the decimal percent times the liters. One equation for total volume, one for total substance, decimals on both sides.

If your system still shows raw percents, it's wrong before you've solved anything.
